power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Safety and tolerability of RJx-01 to maintain muscle integrity in patients following hospitalisation with an acute exacerbation of COPD (MINT-COPD): protocol for a phase IIa randomised double-blind placebo-controlled trial Names of protocol contributors (3a)
Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (COPD) is one of the leading causes of global disability and disability-adjusted life years.
One of the key systemic features of COPD is impaired skeletal muscle mass and function, termed sarcopenia.

The recognition of skeletal muscle dysfunction as a treatable trait in COPD opens a therapeutic avenue for pharmacological development, with the aim of improving physical function and reducing healthcare utilisation.
A novel combination drug, RJx-01, was identified as a candidate therapy for sarcopenia based on preclinical evidence.

The primary aim of this study is to evaluate the safety and tolerability of RJx-01 compared with placebo following hospitalisation with an acute exacerbation of COPD (AECOPD), when acute deterioration of skeletal muscle integrity is observed.
Exploratory efficacy analyses will assess differences in muscle function, mass, and multi-omic-derived outcomes.
The MINT-COPD trial is a phase IIa, single centre, randomised controlled trial (RCT).
Eighty participants admitted to hospital with AECOPD will be randomly assigned 1:1 to receive either oral RJx-01 or placebo, once daily for 24 weeks.
The primary outcome is safety and tolerability of RJx-01 compared with placebo in COPD patients.

Exploratory objectives aim to assess the preliminary effects of AECOPD-associated hospitalisation and RJx-01 treatment on muscle mass, function, and fatiguability, as well as patient reported symptoms and frailty.
The optional skeletal muscle biopsy sub-study aims to assess the effects of AECOPD on proteomic and transcriptomic markers of skeletal muscle.
Ethical approval for this study was granted on 28-MAR-2025 by the East Midlands -Leicester Central Research Ethics Committee (ref: 25/EM/0032).
The MINT-COPD trial commenced recruitment in May 2025 and aims establish the safety profile of RJx-01 in a population of individuals admitted to hospital with AECOPD.
The results of the trial will be disseminated through publication in relevant peer-reviewed journals.

Skeletal muscle dysfunction in COPD independently predicts mortality, readmission and disability, and hospitalisation for an acute exacerbation causes further muscle loss that does not immediately recover.
Exercise-based rehabilitation may help but is completed by fewer than 10% of patients after an exacerbation.
RJx-01, a fixed-dose combination of metformin and galantamine, has improved muscle function in preclinical ageing models and attenuated disuse-related strength loss in healthy older adults.
This Phase IIa study is the first to test its safety and tolerability in people hospitalised with an exacerbation of COPD.
The findings will establish whether treatment with RJx-01 is feasible in an acutely unwell, multimorbid population.
An acceptable safety profile would provide the basis for an adequately powered efficacy trial and support further evaluation of skeletal muscle as a treatable trait in COPD.
To date, no pharmacological therapy is licensed to reduce physical or functional decline or reduce the risk of sarcopenia.
Therefore, the intervention in this study will be provided solely as an adjunct to participants' usual care, with no active comparator.
A placebo group is required to address potential intervention biases both among the participants and the investigators.
The primary objective is to evaluate the safety and tolerability of RJx-01 versus placebo between day 1 and week 28 following hospitalisation with AECOPD (24 weeks' treatment and 4 weeks' follow-up).

Outcomes include Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events (CTCAE) grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs) and serious adverse events (SAEs) at least possibly related to the investigational medicinal product (IMP), all-cause hospital admissions, and mortality.

Exploratory objectives will assess effects on further safety and tolerability outcomes, physical function, muscle strength, fatiguability, muscle mass, quality of life, frailty status, biomarkers, lung function, physical activity, mortality, and healthcare utilisation.
A muscle biopsy sub-study will explore skeletal muscle multi-omics and structure in a subset of participants.
This is an assessor and participant-blinded, randomised, placebo-controlled, parallelgroup, phase IIa clinical trial.
Participants will be randomised using a 1:1 ratio to either RJx-01 or placebo.
The trial design follows an exploratory, superiority framework focused on determining safety and tolerability, with exploratory evaluation of preliminary efficacy.
Trial setting (13)
The single-centre trial will be conducted at Glenfield Hospital, University Hospitals of Leicester NHS Trust, Leicester, UK.
Participants will be recruited following admission to the Clinical Decisions Unit (CDU) with a primary clinician-defined diagnosis of an acute exacerbation of COPD.

Gender will be recorded as self-reported using the categories: male (including trans man); female (including trans woman); non-binary; other (not listed); not known; and not stated.
Race, ethnicity and ancestry Race and ethnicity will be collected as a selfreported variable using the categories included in the study case report form.
In the final trial report, race will be presented exactly as recorded, without aggregation of categories.
Socioeconomic status Socioeconomic status (SES) is not collected in this study.
No SES-specific indicators (e.g., deprivation indices, income bands, occupation, or education level) are captured in the CRF, and SES cannot be inferred from other recorded variables.

Geographic location Participants will be recruited from Leicester, a predominantly urban area, with the study population reflecting a wider catchment that includes suburban and semi-rural communities across Leicestershire.
As this is a single-site trial, specific geographical grouping of participants will not be reported.
In addition to demographic variables, diseaserelated characteristics including FEV1/FVC ratio, mMRC category, smoking history, and exacerbation history (e.g. prior hospitalisations for AECOPD).
Comorbidities (excluding COPD) will be reported categorically.

Additional consent provisions for collection and use of participant data and biological specimens (32b)
Participants will consent to the collection, storage and analysis of samples (including DNA analysis) and use of de-identified data and images.
De-identified data and samples may be shared with academic or commercial partners for trial-related analyses.

Optional consent will be sought for future ethically approved research use of de-identified data, tissue banking of leftover samples, future genetic analysis, contact about future studies and a results summary.
Investigational Medicinal Product (IMP):
Participants in the IMP (active) arm of the trial will receive RJx-01 (Rejuvenate Biomed NV, Diepenbeek, Belgium) via oral self-administration, once daily for 24 weeks.

The trial IMP consists of a combination of metformin hydrochloride (MET) modified release, an antihyperglycemic agent that improves insulin sensitivity and reduces hepatic glucose production, and galantamine hydrobromide (GAL) immediate release, a reversible acetylcholinesterase inhibitor that increases central cholinergic neurotransmission.
The IMP will be supplied in pre-labelled kits by the hospital pharmacy, with written dosing and storage instructions.
The first dose will be given when participants are medically fit for discharge, with subsequent doses self-administered at home.
A low dose will be taken for 7 days to reduce gastrointestinal and cholinergic side effects, increasing to a maintenance dose after face-to-face medical review.
Safety and tolerability will be monitored at monthly visits and by telephone.
Placebo (comparator):
The placebo comprises pre-labelled treatment kits containing inactive ingredients only, matched to the IMP in appearance, packaging, and labelling.

Tissue will undergo comprehensive cellular and molecular analysis including transcriptional profiling, proteomics, immunohistochemistry, and electron microscopy to characterise the skeletal muscle phenotype.

As there is no specific antidote for RJx-01 or its components, management would be primarily supportive, so unblinding would rarely alter immediate treatment.

All outcome assessments (summarised in the supplementary material) will follow standard operating procedures.
Specialist assessments (e.g. isokinetic dynamometry, DXA, MRI) will be performed by qualified operators using calibrated equipment.

The primary safety analysis will compare rates of IMP-related AEs of grade ≥3, IMPrelated SAEs, IMP-related hospitalisations and deaths between treatment arms.
Only events with onset on or after the first administration of the investigational medicinal product will be included; events with an unknown start date will be classified as treatment emergent.
Treatment groups will be compared using a Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test for general association, controlling for stratification factors.

For exploratory efficacy outcomes, continuous endpoints will be analysed using a mixed model for repeated measures with baseline value, stratification factors, treatment, time, and treatment-by-time interaction as fixed effects and participant as a random effect.
Nonparametric alternatives will be used where distributional assumptions are not met.
Withingroup differences versus baseline will be tested using a paired t-test or Wilcoxon signed ranks test.
Categorical endpoints will be compared using the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel test for general association.
Time-to-readmission will be summarised using Kaplan-Meier methods and compared using the stratified log-rank test.
The primary safety analysis will include all randomised participants who receive at least one dose of the IMP or placebo.

Exploratory efficacy analyses will be conducted on the intent-to-treat population containing all randomised participants who receive at least one dose of the IMP or placebo and who have post-baseline data.
A summary of participant flow including numbers screened, screen-failed, randomised, exposed, discontinued (with reasons), and completed will be reported in accordance with the CONSORT statement.
The mixed model for repeated measures used for continuous exploratory endpoints assumes data are missing at random and uses all available observations without imputation.

Pre-specified intercurrent event strategies will be applied: treatment policy for rehospitalisation, retaining data during and after readmission, and while-on-treatment for death and IMP discontinuation, using data up to the event.
Sensitivity analyses under alternative missing data assumptions will be detailed in the statistical analysis plan.

Baseline demographics and clinical characteristics will be summarised by treatment arm using means, standard deviations, medians, and quartiles for continuous variables and frequencies and percentages for categorical variables.
Concurrent treatments (pharmacological and non-pharmacological) and important protocol deviations will be tabulated by treatment arm.
Any pre-specified subgroup or sensitivity analyses will be detailed in the statistical analysis plan, which will be finalised prior to database lock.
No formal interim analysis is planned for this trial outside of the safety analyses provided to the DSMC, which is prepared by an independent unblinded statistician.
The full study protocol is available upon request.

Physical frailty and sarcopenia represent major clinical burdens in chronic respiratory disease, with consequences that extend beyond reduced quality of life and functional independence to poorer prognosis and elevated risk of re-hospitalisation. (12, 25) Previous pharmacological approaches targeting muscle size in COPD via anabolic pathways have failed to demonstrate concomitant improvements in functional capacity and health status. (26) (27) (28) Exploring alternative therapeutic pathways is therefore a clear next step.

text.text: RJx-01 provides a candidate novel approach to address a specific mechanistic pathway of muscle dysfunction occurring in COPD patients.

Building on synergistic effects for skeletal muscle in preclinical models and in healthy older adults undergoing immobilisation, the combination -further supported by an optimised low dose formulation -is hypothesised to demonstrate a favourable safety and tolerability profile alongside a preliminary efficacy signal for skeletal muscle outcomes in patients hospitalised with AECOPD.
MINT-COPD will employ a two-arm, randomised, placebo-controlled design, as no pharmacological standard of care exists for skeletal muscle dysfunction in this setting.
Whilst the primary objective is to evaluate safety and tolerability, robust physiological assessments will also explore preliminary effects on skeletal muscle integrity.

Despite the absence of a formal sample size calculation, a recruitment target of 80 is deemed sufficient to detect signs of meaningful differences in many of the key strength and functional outcomes, based on effect sizes from previous interventional studies. (29) (30) (31) This trial will also represent one of the most detailed longitudinal assessments of skeletal muscle recovery following hospitalisation for AECOPD, providing unique insights into postexacerbation recovery trajectories.
